chunks: "A half-bridge is just two switches stacked in series between the supply and ground, and the output comes from the node between them.
The top one is the high-side switch, the bottom one is the low-side switch.
If the high side is on, the output is at the supply; if the low side is on, it's at ground; if both are off, the output floats and the load current finds its own way through a body diode.
For a real one I'd use two NFETs. Low side has its source at ground, easy to drive.
High side has its drain at the supply and its source on the output, so its gate has to go a few volts above the supply, which means a gate driver with a bootstrap capacitor.
I draw the body diode on both FETs because the load is inductive.
I show the load from the output node to ground, or to the supply, or to a mid-point made of two capacitors if I need both polarities.
The controller turns on one FET, turns it off, waits a bit of dead time, then turns on the other.
The dead time is there so the two can never be on at once, which would short the supply.
The average output is duty cycle times supply, and if I put an inductor and capacitor after it I've just drawn a buck converter."
